newsitem.title: DUBAI: Moslem world prepares for Ramadan fasting month.
newsitem.headline: Moslem world prepares for Ramadan fasting month.

text.p: The world's Moslem community of a billion people in more than 50 countries prepared on Thursday to observe the start of the sacred fasting month Ramadan.

In most Islamic countries, the month during which the faithful fast during daylight hours traditionally starts one day after the sighting of the new moon there. As a result, Ramadan usually starts on two or three different days in different countries.
Saudi Arabia, birthplace of Islam in the seventh century and home to the religion's two holiest shrines, and many other Islamic countries have announced Ramadan would begin on Friday.

People are warned not to eat, drink or smoke in public even if they are not Moslems or not fasting themselves. All sensual pleasures, including sex and listening to music, are forbidden during the day. Non-practising Moslems tend to avoid alcohol, gambling and other un-Islamic activities.
During Ramadan government offices and some private companies observe shorter working hours.

Saudi Arabia's Interior Ministry warned non-Moslems to respect the holy month and said foreigners eating, drinking or smoking in public during daylight hours would risk deportation and an end to their work contracts.
It asked all companies employing non-Moslems to "explain all that to them and warn them against commiting any violations".
One-third of Saudi Arabia's 18 million population is expatriate, many of them labourers from the Indian subcontinent and other Asian countries. It is not known how many of them are non-Moslems.
In Kabul, Afghanistan's purist Sunni Moslem Taleban government issued guidelines confining most women to their homes and banning public eating and entertainment.

"Our esteemed sisters are asked not to venture out of their houses without a legal excuse. In case they have to leave their houses they should be veiled from the head to below the ankle," the department for promoting good and suppressing vice said.
"If a man sees a woman during Ramadan, he will be provoked," said the department's deputy head Mullah Enayatullah Baligh.
In Indonesia, the world's biggest Moslem county, fasting starts also on Friday.
Indonesia, like Saudi Arabia and most other Moslem states, is dominated by the majority Sunni sect of Islam.
Ramadan in Iran, the biggest Shi'ite Moslem country, starts on Saturday according to the official calendar, though that is subject to confirmation of the sighting of the new moon.
Every Ramadan Iranian newspapers report dozens of people arrested for flouting the ban on eating and smoking in public, some of whom are lashed on orders of Islamic courts.
Ramadan is the ninth lunar month of the Arab and Islamic calendar which ends this year around May 6.
The name originally meant "great heat" and dated from the solar calendar before the birth of Islam.

Ramadan fasting ends with Eid al-Fitr, a religious feast on the first day of the next month when Moslems formally break their fast. Eid al-Fitr usually involves the exchange of gifts and gold souks typically see an increase in retail jewellery business.
